description: Este no es un grupo, es una familia que albergan personas con cualidades estraordinarias en progracion, resolucion de problemas, trabajo en equipo, comunicacion asertiva. Aqui no solo se programa o solucionan problemas, sino se aprende y se establecen relaciones.
summary: Ad-Astra is an interactive survival game where kids command a Moon or Mars outpost over a series of nights, choosing a destination and a loadout, then spending limited tasks and battery power on shielding, repairs, panel cleaning, rest and sending science data to Earth. It addresses the challenge by making every decision carry a real cost: reinforcing the shield drains battery and food, machines burn power every second, and forecasts of solar storms, dust and cold force players to plan ahead. An in-game panel grounds the experience in real NASA data, including DONKI solar-flare classes, radiation doses measured on the Moon and Mars, signal delay to Mars and the 2018 dust storm, with plain-language explanations of each term. This matters because it turns the genuine trade-offs of deep-space survival into play, so kids can fail safely, try new strategies and leave understanding how real mission planners balance power, oxygen, food and radiation.
details:
What does the project do, and how does it work?

Ad-Astra is an educational survival and resource-management game in which players command a crewed base on Mars or the Moon. The objective is to keep the crew alive throughout a mission while producing scientific results and transmitting them to Earth. Surviving alone does not fulfill the scientific objective.

Players begin by selecting a destination, a difficulty level, and a supply package. Each choice changes the conditions they must manage. During the mission, they monitor energy, oxygen, food, shielding, health, and, depending on difficulty, additional systems such as structural integrity and solar-panel condition. Crew morale also affects how much work can be done.

The game combines a nightly decision cycle with resource changes that occur while the player acts. Machines generate food or oxygen but consume power. Tasks such as repairs, experiments, and shielding improvements compete for limited actions and supplies. In the more complex modes, players must also direct the antenna and upload stored research data. Equipment failures, solar hazards, and other events force them to revise their plans. A mission report shows resource histories, influential decisions, and lessons from the outcome.

What benefits does it have?

Ad-Astra makes trade-offs visible. Players can observe why running every machine continuously is unsustainable, why research depends on life support, and why protecting equipment matters. Instead of treating resources as separate numbers, the game presents them as an interconnected system.

The prototype includes a guided introduction, explanations of scientific terms, and three difficulty levels intended for ages 7–9, 10–12, and 13 and above. These levels introduce different amounts of complexity. The final report gives players material for discussing what went wrong and what they might change in another attempt.

Stored solar-flare records allow the game to continue when live data cannot be downloaded. This keeps the core experience playable without a reliable connection.

What is the intended impact?

The intended impact is to encourage curiosity about space science and give young players practice with planning, prioritization, and reasoning about consequences. By placing responsibility for a crew in the player’s hands, Ad-Astra connects technical systems with human needs such as food, health, rest, and communication.

The game could support classroom discussions or informal learning activities about radiation, energy, scientific research, and the challenges of distant missions. These are intended applications rather than demonstrated outcomes. Testing with learners and educators would be needed to assess usability, age suitability, and learning impact.

What tools did we use?

The playable prototype was developed in Unity 2021.3 using C#. Its scripts implement the simulation, mission events, interface, tutorial, audio behavior, and mission review. The interface uses Unity UI and programmatically created visual elements. The project also includes the HauntedPSX render pipeline for its retro visual presentation.

NASA’s DONKI API supplies recent solar-flare records when available, alongside a curated archive used as a fallback. Scientific explanations reference radiation measurements from Curiosity on Mars and Chang’e-4 on the Moon, as well as communication delays and NASA’s Deep Space Network. These references inform the experience; they do not make every game value a direct scientific measurement. The project mentions NASA’s Open Science Data Repository, but does not currently use its experimental numerical datasets in the simulation.

How is the project creative?

Ad-Astra turns scientific information into a source of gameplay pressure. A solar flare is more than a fact to read: it becomes a reason to prepare shielding and reconsider priorities. Research also has a practical journey, from conducting an experiment to storing and transmitting its results.

The mission-control presentation uses animated icons, resource indicators, radio-style guidance, alerts, and retro screen effects to make the player feel responsible for an operating base. The contrast between scientific ambition and immediate survival creates the central tension: the most productive choice is not always the safest one.

What factors did the team consider?

What factors did the team consider? The design reflects several practical considerations: how much complexity different players can handle, how clearly the interface communicates danger, and how to make resource decisions consequential without requiring specialist knowledge. Difficulty settings and optional guidance provide different entry points into the same core experience.

Scientific clarity is another consideration. The game distinguishes real reference information from simplified mechanics: mission time is compressed, resource values are normalized, and communication delays are adapted to the decision cycle. Solar-flare records inspire hazards rather than providing a full physical forecast of conditions at a base.

Finally, the experience considers unreliable connectivity, replayability, and feedback after failure. Different destinations, starting supplies, and events create reasons to try another strategy. Further development should test whether players understand the alerts and trade-offs, whether the difficulty feels fair, and which parts of the experience best support the intended learning goals.y
